title: NASA is Full Steam Ahead on Artemis III, IV and V - Space Policy Online
content: NASA officials projected confidence today in their plans to launch the Artemis III earth-orbital test flight in mid-2027 and land American astronauts on the Moon in 2028.  Whether SpaceX’s Starship or Blue Origin’s Blue Moon MK2 gets there first is up in the air, but NASA expects both will deliver crews to the surface by the end of that year. The South Pole is still the destination, but they acknowledged more data is needed from robotic landers before making a final decision. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman was joined by Associate Administrator and Chief Engineer Amit Kshatriya and Artemis Program Manager Jeremy Parsons in explaining how efforts to return Americans to the lunar surface have evolved over the years. With the changes initiated this year in accelerating the pace of Artemis launches and revamping the NASA workforce by in-boarding contractors, they firmly believe they can meet the deadlines. In December 2025 as Isaacman was sworn in as NASA Administrator, the Artemis II mission was getting ready to send four astronauts around the Moon and the next mission, Artemis III, was targeted as the flight that would land astronauts on the surface. A month before Artemis II lifted off, Isaacman made a course correction for the next flights. Artemis III would be an earth-orbiting test in mid-2027 of rendezvous and docking procedures with the two Human Landing Systems being built by SpaceX and Blue Origin. Artemis IV and Artemis V would return astronauts to the surface, both in 2028. The deadlines are viewed as ambitious because progress appears slow on the Human Landing Systems (HLSs) needed to ferry the crews between lunar orbit and the surface, and on the spacesuits they need to wear when they exit the lander. Axiom Space is building the suits. Concerns also have emerged about the choice of the South Pole as the landing site. Not only has it been more than 50 years since NASA landed anyone on the Moon, but it was with a different type of vehicle and in comparatively safe areas closer to the equator. The South Pole is an entirely different environment with steep slopes, low Sun angles, and temperature extremes and fewer mission abort options. NASA wants to go there because water ice deposited by comets over the eons is thought to be accessible in permanently shadowed regions. The water ice possibly could be extracted to support human outposts or create propellant for rockets travelling further into space. Today’s briefing was a progress update. The bottom line is NASA is going full steam ahead on mid-2027 for Artemis III and 2028 for Artemis IV and V. In a note to the NASA workforce in September, Isaacman said the mid-2027 date was “90 days broken to schedule,” but explained today that internal message was intended to galvanize the workforce to find solutions. All three speakers repeatedly praised the NASA and contractor workforce for doing just that and Artemis III is still expected in mid-2027. Test versions of Blue Origin’s Blue Moon MK2 and SpaceX’s Starship will dock with NASA’s Orion spacecraft in earth orbit. Blue Origin’s Blue Moon MK2 can loiter in orbit for up to 30 days, so will launch first. Next is Orion on a NASA Space Launch System (SLS) rocket with a “spacer” instead of the Interim Cryogenic Propulsion Stage used for Artemis II since it doesn’t need to depart earth orbit. Orion and Blue Moon MK2 will dock on Day 3 and spend two days together while the crew enters the lander and a variety of tests are conducted. Starship will launch on Day 6. The only change from other Starships is that it will have a passive docking system on the nose. Orion will spend only 2 hours docked to Starship and the crew will not enter it. Uncrewed test flights of both HLSs are required to demonstrate they can safely land on the Moon. Starship requires in-space propellant transfer to leave earth orbit. A fuel depot is needed where cryogenic propellant can be aggregated and replenished to compensate for boil-off. Earth-orbiting fuel depots don’t exist yet and in-space cryogenic fuel transfer hasn’t been demonstrated. SpaceX anticipates doing that for the first time early next year, and the uncrewed lunar landing test in late 2027. For the 2028 lunar landing, the fully-fueled Starship will dock with Orion in earth orbit and push it to the Moon rather than meeting Orion in lunar orbit as originally planned. Once there, two crew members will transfer into the lander and make the trip down and back, returning to Earth in Orion. Originally Blue Origin also planned to use in-space propellant transfer to reach the Moon, but they’ve modified their approach. Now, they will use three of their smaller Blue Moon MK1 spacecraft as tugs to get the Blue Moon MK2 lander to lunar orbit where it will meet up with Orion. As with Starship, two crew members will transfer into the lander to go down and back, and return home on Orion. Like the landers, Axiom’s spacesuits are behind schedule. NASA recently changed the requirements to allow a simpler, lighter “sortie” suit. The crews will only be able to spend two hours on the surface, on two excursions, but NASA considers that acceptable for the first missions. Yesterday, NASA’s Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel raised a number of concerns about plans for Artemis IV and beyond including the readiness of the landers, the requirement for only one uncrewed landing test for each provider, and the fact this will be the first time cryogenic propellants are used on the Moon (Apollo used hypergolics). Concerns also have been expressed about choosing the South Pole for the first lunar landing in more than 50 years instead of an easier-to-reach location closer to the equator with smoother terrain. The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) released a NASA-requested report earlier this week identifying four non-polar sites that would yield valuable scientific results. Asked today if NASA is considering other landing spots, Kshatryia acknowledged there’s a lot of unknowns about the South Pole and “we will always debate” the best landing spot. More data is needed and that will come from the Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) robotic missions that have landed already and others planned between now and when crews arrive. Isaacman added the South Pole “is probably the most advantageous area” and the CLPS landings will provide “a really good understanding of the environment” so that’s what they’re tracking right now. He also agreed, however, that returning to one of the Apollo landing sites as recommended in the NASEM report would be “very cool at some point in the future.” SpacePolicyOnline.com has the right (but not the obligation) to monitor the comments and to remove any materials it deems inappropriate.  We do not post comments that include links to other websites since we have no control over that content nor can we verify the security of such links.

title: Gloucester v Bath: Five takeaways as Finn Russell 'silenced' by the Shed - Planet Rugby
content: Jac Morgan and Finn Russell in action during Gloucester v Bath in the Gallagher PREM. Following a 23-5 victory for Gloucester over Bath, here are our five takeaways from the Gallagher PREM encounter at Kingsholm on Friday. Gloucester earned the derby spoils over their West Country rivals with a fantastic defensive display against Bath as they claimed their third victory in four league games. Almost three years ago, Finn Russell famously shushed the Shed, but this time it was the Cherry and White supporters who were putting their fingers to their lips as the maverick Scotland fly-half was silenced by a magnificent effort from the hosts. Led by the ubiquitous Wales star Jac Morgan, Gloucester withstood wave after wave of Bath attacks and were ultimately clinical when the opportunities came their way. George Barton was on target with three quick-fire penalties as the home side moved 9-0 ahead in the first half before the visitors responded via Kepu Tuipulotu’s try on the stroke of half-time. That was the only score the 2024/2025 PREM champions could muster, despite the plethora of chances that came their way. They constantly coughed up possession when inside the opposition 22, which was in stark contrast to the Cherry and Whites, who sealed the win through Freddie Thomas and Max Llewellyn tries. It seemed like defence coaches were allowed to run the sessions this week. After the recent spate of high scores and porous English defences, which led to plenty of criticism following their Investec Champions Cup struggles last weekend, it felt like we had stepped back in time. Granted, Storm Austen helped the rearguards to an extent as the wind and rain made it difficult for both teams, but it was more about the willingness of both West Country clubs to put their bodies on the line. Gloucester were one of the few PREM sides to emerge with some credit in the aftermath of the first round of European action, earning a creditable draw with back-to-back champions Bordeaux-Bègles, and the grit they showed then was very much in evidence on Friday. While we all revel in watching teams attack with vigour, it was refreshing to see an almost old-school contest at Kingsholm. What’s more, it did not detract from a fantastic contest where the physicality and sheer defensive desperation, especially from the Cherry and Whites, was just as enjoyable as the free-flowing rugby there has been at the start of the season. One of the best things about this sport is the variety, while England boss Steve Borthwick probably enjoyed that more than the try-fests he’s watched previously. For half an hour of this game it was scoreless, thanks mainly to a stunning defensive effort from the Cherry and Whites, who withstood a barrage of attacks from Bath. Their infringements close to the tryline led to yellow cards for Ollie Thorley and Ciaran Knight, but the hosts remained firm with the visitors having two tries disallowed in the first half. In fact, Gloucester opened the scoring with those players off the field before Barton kicked two more penalties to extend their buffer to nine. Only at the end of the opening period were George Skivington’s men breached, ironically after Thorley and Knight had returned, but they still did incredibly well to reach the interval ahead. Half-time offered only brief respite as Bath continued to pound the Gloucester line, resulting in another sin-binning, this time to Will Joseph, but once again the home side remained resolute and resisted their arch-rivals. It was that resilience in the face of adversity which proved utterly vital in this victory and suggested they are genuine contenders this season. Project Chariot explained: the secret RFU and Premiership Rugby merger plan that could return after the World Cup While the Gloucester rearguard has quite rightly been praised, Bath supporters, coaches and players will once again be frustrated by their misfiring attack. Despite containing the genius that is Russell and producing some positive moments at the start of this campaign, it is fair to say they have not been nearly as fluent since the departure of Lee Blackett. The defeat against Montpellier, where they failed to take advantage of several promising positions, was frustrating, but this loss points to a bigger issue at the heart of Bath’s game. Granted, the conditions were not easy but, in their limited opportunities with ball in hand, the Cherry and Whites were far more incisive. In contrast, Johann van Graan’s men were uninspiring and one-dimensional. Not too many fancied Gloucester to do much this season but their recruitment was objectively excellent. While Wales have been utterly hopeless for the past three years, there is no doubt that Dewi Lake and Morgan are of Test class – albeit the former was absent for Friday’s game. Most importantly, they are leaders and have ultimately brought higher standards to this Cherry and Whites outfit. Morgan was particularly excellent and led their defensive effort alongside the similarly destructive Jean Kleyn, who is another newcomer at Kingsholm. They were ably supported by the equally industrious academy graduates, with Thomas, Jack Clement and Arthur Clark all vital to this victory. It was that pack effort which proved decisive, but credit must also go to Barton at full-back, who kicked 13 points and was good on both sides of the ball in difficult conditions. He is a player who has stepped up significantly this season and is now a mainstay of that Gloucester XV. As for Bath, there were some positive individual contributions with 20-year-old Enoch Opoku-Gyamfi looking like an incredible talent for Italy in the second-row. The likes of Josh Bayliss, Tuipulotu, despite his lineout wobbles, Beno Obano and Archie Griffin also had their moments, but as a collective they faltered. title: Cadillac's $239,000 Escalade-V Anniversary Edition Is One Expensive Beast - Yahoo Autos
content: The Cadillac Escalade-V has never been particularly subtle, but the American luxury brand has found a way to make its flagship performance SUV even more extravagant. Meet the 2027 Escalade-V 125th Anniversary Collector Series, a limited-production special edition with an eye-watering price tag. Unveiled ahead of the 2026 United States Grand Prix in Austin, Texas, the anniversary model celebrates 125 years since Cadillac's founding in 1902. It combines the Escalade-V's imposing presence with exclusive styling details and an unusually high level of personalization. Only 252 examples will be produced, making this one of the rarest versions of the Escalade yet. Buyers will even be able to select their vehicle's identification number and commemorative serial number, subject to availability, adding another layer of exclusivity. However, exclusivity comes at a substantial cost. Cadillac has priced the anniversary edition at approximately $239,000, making it roughly $70,000 more expensive than a regular Escalade-V. The Collector Series is available in two exterior finishes: exclusive Midnight Stone Frost and Vibrant White Tricoat. Both are complemented by dark exterior badging, blue brake calipers, and distinctive forged 24-inch wheels. Carbon fiber features prominently, appearing on the grille surround, mirror caps, lower rear fascia, and engine cover. Cadillac also adds heritage-inspired V8 puddle lamps and commemorative details celebrating the company's history. Inside, the anniversary Escalade-V features a two-tone Black and Sheer Gray interior accented by Santorini Blue stitching. The striking blue theme extends to the seat belts and even the vehicle's exclusive key fob. Additional touches include illuminated anniversary sill plates, special interior badging, and Collector Series floor mats. Cadillac says the blue accents reference its V-Series performance heritage and racing-inspired design language. Although the anniversary treatment focuses primarily on exclusivity and appearance, the Escalade-V's underlying performance credentials are still a major attraction. The regular model's supercharged 6.2-liter V8 produces 682 horsepower and 653 lb-ft of torque. Cadillac hasn't announced any mechanical upgrades specifically for the Collector Series, suggesting buyers are paying for rarity and distinctive finishes rather than additional performance. Given the Escalade-V's already formidable output, that probably won't disappoint many enthusiasts. Cadillac is accepting orders for the anniversary edition in the United States and Canada, with pricing starting at approximately $239,000 before taxes and dealer fees. Final transaction prices will be determined by individual dealerships. For collectors who want one of the most exclusive Escalades ever offered, the 125th Anniversary Collector Series certainly makes a statement. Whether its unique styling and limited production justify the substantial premium is another question entirely. title: Hull v Brentford team news: Andrews provides Schuster, Jensen and Collins updates - Brentford FC
content:
Brentford head coach Keith Andrews provides updates on Jannik Schuster, Mathias Jensen and Nathan Collins ahead of the Bees' Premier League trip to Hull City (2pm kick-off GMT), live on Sky Sports; Andrews also discusses Sunday's test against the Tigers, as well as former Brentford captain John Egan Schuster was withdrawn at half-time of Brentford's 2-2 draw at Aston Villa earlier this month before missing the Liverpool defeat. "Jannik just had a bit of a troubled week going into the Liverpool game, really," Andrews explained. "A bit of a knock from international duty crept up on him during the Villa game, and then he wasn't particularly well for a few days, so it was just a very disruptive week. "But he's been back training the last few days, so he's back to himself, more or less." Andrews reported no fresh major injury concerns, and was also encouraged by the progress of Collins and Jensen. "There's nothing major to note; we're pretty much as we were last weekend," he continued. "Some players have taken the next step of their journey back with really good weeks of training. Nathan, in particular, and Mathias Jensen made another really good step with training, considering that he's only been back a week or two." Brentford travel to a Hull side who have made a good start to the campaign following promotion to the Premier League, taking nine points from their opening seven fixtures. Andrews believes the Tigers' spirit and belief have been central to their strong return to the top flight. "I think they've been brilliant," he said. "It's very evident that they have a spirit, a really honest spirit about the group, and they have a togetherness and honesty about the group. "They've got some very, very experienced players that have been in the league before, and they've got players that are there for the first time that want to enjoy the journey. "The way they play the game and the way they're organised is very impressive." Looking ahead to Sunday's game at MKM Stadium, Andrews added: "I expect a proper test, a way of playing that can be very testing. "They have a belief that they can absolutely compete at this level. They've shown that they can, week in, week out. "They've produced some really, really good performances and they've been in every single game they've played in." Sunday's fixture could also see Brentford reunited with former captain John Egan, who has played an important role for Hull following their promotion. Andrews knows the Republic of Ireland defender well, having coached him at international level and during his time at Sheffield United. “He's someone that I really like as a man,” said Andrews on the former Bees skipper, who made 71 appearances and scored seven goals during two seasons with Brentford between 2016 and 2018. "I coached him at international level and I also coached him at Sheffield United, so I know John pretty well. "I'm so happy for him that he's made that move to Hull, got the promotion back, playing at the highest level and still playing a really important role for our country. "He's a player you would go into the trenches with. He's been a magnificent player. He's a man that I really admire and like." Vantage London

title: Billy V Live: Spotlighting local filmmakers at HIFF and developing ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi Sign Language - Hawaii News Now
content: HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - On this week’s episode of Billy V Live, host Billy V shared with us two impactful interviews: Hawaiʻi filmmakers showcasing new work at the Hawaiʻi International Film Festival, and advocates working to create access to ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi for deaf keiki. Writer-director David Rowlands joined composer William Watson and actor-producer Kyla Hee to discuss two new productions premiering at HIFF: Light a Fire in Me, a feature-length psychological thriller, and My Love?, a psychological horror short. Both projects were produced and shot in Hawaiʻi with a local cast and crew. Rowlands said Light a Fire in Me explores the darker, urban side of Hawaiʻi and how toxicity in relationships can spread if left unaddressed, while My Love leans surrealist, blurring what is real and not real. The two films were shot in Hawaiʻi with a 95% local cast and crew. The projects will premiere on November 5 at Consolidated Theatres Kāhala. Visit HIFF.org for more information. In the second interview, Billy V featured a local project that is creating Hawaiian language hand signs to help Deaf and hearing keiki connect through ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi. Billy spoke with co-founders Kekai Kaaumoana-Cummings and Keane Waian Nakapueo-Garcia, alongside parent advocate Nikki Kepoo and interpreter Hercules Goss-Kuehn about the mission behind ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi Kuhi Lima (OHKL). Cummings, who is deaf and began learning ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi at UH Mānoa, said he realized the deaf lāhui had almost no access to the Hawaiian language and culture, prompting him to help develop kuhilima with Garcia. The group says the long-term goal is more than accommodation. It is to provide deaf keiki with a way to connect to the Hawaiian language and culture. Kaaumoana-Cummings also shares sign language tutorials and educational content on social media, including TikTok and Instagram, to raise broader awareness for the Deaf community within the lāhui. title: Arsenal v Everton: Key stats and talking points - AOL.com
content: Finishing was a problem last weekend for Arsenal, who had 74% possession but only one shot on target against Nottingham Forest. It was one of their "finishers", as manager Mikel Arteta likes to call substitutes, who yet again saved the day. That shot from Noni Madueke, which deflected into the Forest net 10 minutes from time, meant that it was their third Premier League victory in a row in which a player from the bench had scored the winner. It may not have been pretty but it was enough for three points, and is further proof of Arteta's ability to make game-changing substitutions. Since the Spaniard's appointment in December 2019, Arsenal have scored more winning goals from substitutes than any other team, and their tally of three this season is already halfway towards the record of six, also set by Arteta's team in 2024-25. It was Arsenal's 32nd 1-0 win in the Premier League of Arteta's tenure, the joint-highest figure in that time frame, along with Everton. So, there might not be goals galore on Saturday - not least because Everton also struggled in attack last weekend against Chelsea, failing to score in a Premier League home game for the first time since February. They had just six shots, their fewest in a Premier League game in nearly a year. They could have their work cut out to improve on that at the Emirates. This season, Arsenal have conceded just five league goals, facing fewer shots on target (21) and having a lower xG against (5.6) than any other side. The Toffees have won just one of their past 30 away Premier League matches against the Gunners, losing 24 of those. Under David Moyes, Everton have never won away at Arsenal in the league in 13 attempts, losing 10 times in that run. But Everton had gone undefeated in the league this season until last weekend, so Moyes will have hope of breaking his Arsenal duck, which would also end his side's eight-game winless run on the road, and could propel the Toffees up into the top five in the Premier League.

title: Chelsea v Tottenham: Key stats and talking points - AOL.com
content: "Very professional, very serious and looking solid," was how manager Xavi Alonso evaluated Chelsea's win at Everton last weekend. The 2-0 victory included what is becoming something of a Chelsea trademark – a quickfire goal, with Pedro Neto scoring at the very start of the second half. That was the third time in the Premier League this season that Alonso's side had scored in the opening minute of either half. But it was what happened at the other end of the pitch that will have surely pleased the Spaniard most, with Chelsea keeping their first clean sheet in the league since January, a run of 23 matches. Alonso pointed out that "it's just one game"; and although Chelsea are in the top four, only five clubs have let in more goals in this season's Premier League, while even two of the three sides in the relegation zone have conceded fewer. The Blues are now aiming for back-to-back clean sheets for the first time since December, and will be hopeful of achieving that against a Tottenham side who have struggled this season, and scored just once away from home. Chelsea have won their past six league matches against Spurs, and have lost just one of their past 16 London derbies at Stamford Bridge. Tottenham fans will be well aware that they have won just one of their past 36 league visits to the Bridge, and have picked up just two points in the past eight trips. Given their record, it is probably never a good time to visit Chelsea, but Spurs did at least finally get a league win this season with their victory over Coventry on Monday. Extra reason to celebrate was Omar Marmoush's first goal since his £59m move from Manchester City, along with the return from long-term injury of Dejan Kulusevski. And the catalyst for the victory was James Maddison, who on his first start for 18 months needed just 14 minutes to make his mark, scoring Spurs' first first-half goal of the season. Their three goals – all of which came from outside the box – doubled their Premier League tally for the season, and earned them just a fourth league win in 2026. But Chelsea is not a happy hunting ground, and the away fans will be fearing Tottenham could lose a seventh consecutive London derby for the first time in their league history.

title: Honda CR-V Hybrid Lease Dispute Takes a Turn After Customer Calls Credit Union - Yahoo Autos
content: A customer leasing a Honda CR-V in Santa Monica says they negotiated a deal for $350 a month, but it suddenly turned into a $460 monthly payment after the dealership claimed their loan was denied. The customer shared their experience on Reddit, explaining that they initially negotiated a lease deal with the dealership for $350 per month with 10,000 miles per year before returning to sign paperwork. However, the customer said they noticed the paperwork only showed 8,000 miles per year. The customer brought the issue up to a manager, and they eventually secured the original terms, leading to them paying a $4,000 deposit and driving off in the vehicle. More than a month later, the customer said the insurance rider was about to expire, and they received no communication from the dealership or Rize Credit Union, which was identified as the lender handling the application. According to the post, a finance employee named Anthony finally contacted the customer and requested proof of income. The customer provided pay stubs and was told Rize denied the application because the documents were considered fake. The customer couldn't believe the explanation, given that their credit score was allegedly more than 790. They returned to the dealership, where they were offered a new lease through Honda Financial Services for $460 per month. When the customer declined the new higher offer, they said they would return the vehicle, but a sales manager reportedly told them that the vehicle had depreciated by $4,500. The customer claimed they were given the choice of paying that amount over three years or forfeiting the $4,000 deposit. According to the post, the customer drove roughly 800 miles in the month they had the CR-V Hybrid and believed the dealership was trying to pressure them into accepting a more expensive agreement. Frustrated by the circumstances, the customer asked to contact Rize directly to verify why the application was denied. They claimed the dealership's employees initially resisted, citing concerns about damaging their relationship with the credit union. The customer obtained the credit union's number and ended up speaking with a Rize manager. 10 minutes later the customer said they were officially approved by the credit union. In the post, the customer said the dealership changed its explanation, claiming Rize had made a counteroffer requiring another $2,000 down payment. But upon calling the credit union again, the customer said that no counteroffer was actually made and the original application was approved. The customer eventually retrieved their keys and drove away after the dealership processed the first month's payment. They later updated the post stating they reported the incident to the Better Business Bureau and the California Attorney General's Office. In the replies, other users suggested bringing the complaint to another level. One commenter recommended the customer contact American Honda directly so the automaker would be aware of the allegations. Another commenter suggested reporting the incident to the California Department of Motor Vehicles, explaining that they had done so after a similar dispute with a dealership. The post does not establish any further updates about the incident or whether the reports filed received a response. title: Liverpool v Brighton: Where to Watch, Match Preview, Kick Off Time & More - Yahoo Sports
content: Liverpool return to league action this weekend as they take on Brighton at Anfield in what is likely to be a high-scoring game. The Reds are fresh off the back of a seven-goal thriller against Villarreal in the Champions League, while Brighton have just beaten rivals Crystal Palace 5-0 in the Premier League and drawn away in the Europa Conference League. The two sides met just under two weeks before Christmas last season, with the Reds coming out on top in that encounter. Hugo Ekitike, who was in re- hot form at the time, scored twice, with a returning Mohamed Salah getting an assist for Ekitike's second goal. The main storyline around this game was the return to the squad for Mo Salah, who, following a public falling out with the manager at the time, Arne Slot. But talks reportedly took place between the pair, and after missing a Champions League game midweek, he returned to the matchday squad, on the bench, against Brighton. Coming off the bench, he got an assist and helped LFC on their way to three huge points against a Brighton side that arguably deserved a lot more from the game than what they got. Andoni Iraola's side comes into this game full of confidence going forward, but question marks surrounding their defensive credibility. Scoring four goals against a strong La Liga side in Villarreal is a very good sign, with several players looking like they are getting better and better, more accustomed to the system and becoming a stronger unit as each game goes by. However, concerns remain about the defence, not necessarily regarding individuals, but more about how the back four are asked to press high and jump out of position, marking man-to-man. This is very effective when completed successfully, but should a team bypass this high press, then there have been far too many occasions where opposition teams have space in behind and a clear run on goal, something that Villarreal exploited multiple times. While the Spanish outfit failed to convert many of their chances, a team like Brighton certainly will, given their goalscoring prowess this campaign. title: Cadillac’s Mexico-Only Sergio Perez-Themed Escalade-V Special Edition Looks a Tad Familiar - Yahoo Autos
content: On Thursday, Cadillac surprised American buyers with a special edition Escalade-V celebrating the brand's 125th anniversary. That was part of the build-up to the United States Grand Prix at the Circuit of the Americas, the company's second of three home Formula 1 races in its inaugural season. Just one day later, Cadillac is celebrating the upcoming Mexican Grand Prix with yet another collectible Escalade-V ... and truth be told, it kind of looks like the earlier one. This Escalade is a tribute to Sergio "Checo" Pérez, the long-time F1 driver who has enjoyed a strong season with Cadillac even as the team has struggled with reliability and pace in its first year. Pérez, a six-time race winner before joining Cadillac, has effectively become the program's lead driver over the course of its inaugural season. Cadillac is honoring that with an Escalade-V that has quite a lot in common with the 125th Anniversary Collector Series variant that the brand showed off Thursday. The contrasting black-and-white color scheme can be had as either a white-on-black or black on white look, two designs that look strikingly similar to the 125th Anniversary models. Both also boast a carbon fiber engine cover, as well as other accents, and very similar-looking 24-inch wheels. The Mexican market model drops the blue accents seen on U.S.-bound 125th Anniversary models, however, opting instead for red brake calipers. Since the two are set for different North American markets, they can effectively be seen as equivalent products for entirely different customer bases. The Edición Checo Pérez is limited to just 11 examples, and each will feature a numbered plaque featuring the driver's signature. That is a significantly lower number than the 252-model production run for the American-market collectible edition, but the price is not all that different from the hefty $239,000 MSRP for the 125th Anniversary model: the model is priced at 4,099,000 pesos, according to Cadillac's Mexican PR site, which works out to roughly $220,000.

title: Cadillac Celebrates Its 125th Birthday with a Limited Run of V-8-Powered Escalades That Each Cost $239K - Car and Driver
content: The 125th Anniversary Collector Series honors Cadillac’s history by dressing a limited run of Escalade-Vs in special-edition attire. In the early 1900s, the Wright brothers were experimenting with flight, Henry Ford was developing the Model T, and Albert Einstein was making finishing touches to his theory of relativity. At the same time, Cadillac was emerging with the 1903 Runabout, which made 10 horsepower from a single-cylinder engine and cost $850—about $33,300 in today’s economy. Next year will mark 125 years since Cadillac’s founding, and a lot has changed since the Runabout’s release. To celebrate the luxury brand’s milestone anniversary, Cadillac is releasing the 2027 Escalade-V 125th Anniversary Collector Series, which will have a very limited production run. See all results for new 2027 Cadillac Escalade / Escalade ESV for sale near 23917 The Anniversary Collector Series is all about exclusivity. While buyers can’t choose much beyond the exterior paint color in terms of the vehicle’s appearance, they can add a bit of personalization by selecting their own VIN and serial number. To complement the Midnight Stone Frost or Vibrant White Tricoat paint, the Escalade-V 125th Anniversary wears forged 24-inch wheels and features blue brake calipers, dark-finish badges, puddle lamps with heritage V-8 graphics, and carbon-fiber details on the grille surround, lower rear fascia, mirror caps, and engine cover. This special edition doesn’t change much under the hood, but the Escalade-V is plenty powerful as-is. A supercharged 6.2-liter V-8 makes 682 horsepower to cart the massive SUV to 60 mph in just 4.3 seconds in our testing. Inside, Santorini Blue stitching and seatbelts connect Cadillac’s racing history with the special-edition Escalade-V. The blue accents pair with a sleek black-and-gray interior, Collector Series floormats, exclusive interior badging, and a blue key fob. The Escalade-V 125th Anniversary Collector Series will be limited to 252 units and sold only in the United States and Canada. Orders are open now, with pricing starting at around $239,000. title: Match guide | Imps v Burnley - Lincoln City Football Club
content: City return to the ProAmpac Stadium to host Burnley on Saturday 24 October (3pm KO). Ahead of the match, we can provide supporters with a guide to plan their visit. With the home stands almost sold-out, we anticipate a busy turnout. If you are planning to visit the ticket office and club shop or Clubhouse please allow sufficient time to do so. These all open at 10am. Arriving early for Saturday’s fixture? Catch Premier League action in the Fan Village as Aston Villa host Manchester City, with kick-off at 12.30pm. Watch the lunchtime clash live on the big screens before heading into the ProAmpac Stadium to get behind the Imps against Burnley. With Manchester City looking to maintain their perfect start to the league campaign, there is plenty to look forward to ahead of kick-off. City are supporting EFL’s Together Against Racism campaign, running from 16 to 26 October, reinforcing the message that racism has no place in football, online or within our communities. The campaign brings together all 72 EFL clubs to challenge racism and promote an inclusive environment where everyone feels welcome, valued and able to enjoy football free from discrimination. Supporters play an important role in tackling racism. Reporting incidents directly to the club as soon as they happen gives staff, stewards and the relevant authorities the best opportunity to identify offenders and take appropriate action. If you witness racism or discrimination at the ProAmpac Stadium, please report it immediately to a steward or through the club’s reporting channels. A minute’s applause will take place prior to kick-off in memory of former players George Peden and John Vaughan. Supporters are invited to join us in celebrating their lives and paying tribute to their memories. City’s new look matchday fan experience features an expanded Fan Village (open from 12noon), upgraded bars and food concessions, and two big screens. The vibrant pre-match hub offers local food and drink vendors, live entertainment and activities for supporters of all ages. There are also some fantastic locally-sourced food options on offer and the Tipsy Imp will be providing a wide range of premium beers and ciders, with a variety of soft drinks also available throughout. Tipsy Imp will provide a wide range of premium beers and ciders. A variety of soft drinks are also available across the Fan Village. There is plenty going on in the Red Imps Community Trust pod. As well as Trust representatives who are happy to chat about the role they play at the club, in addition to collectible programmes and memorabilia - with donations raising money for Lincoln City Foundation. City's new coffee shop and community space will be open to supporters from 10am, giving fans the chance to experience the new space both pre and post match (until 5.30pm). The new community space is conveniently located next to the club shop, providing the perfect place for supporters, visitors and the local community to relax and refuel. Serving premium coffee from local specialists Seven Districts, the Clubhouse has hot and cold drinks, paninis and sandwiches, as well as a selection of cakes and sweet treats. Prepare for the colder months with the latest winter essentials, available now in the club shop. From winter coats, raincoats, combination jackets and gilets to handy accessories including Imps bobble hats, there is everything you need to stay warm and show your support for City this winter. Visit the club shop before kick-off to browse the latest range. Poacher's Den, situated in the Co-Op Community Hub in the Stacey West Stand, will be open from 12noon with plenty of family-friendly activities. Head to the Fan Village before the match where there are fun family-friendly activities, plus free football sessions on the 3G astro pitch. There's no need to book on - just turn up from 12.30pm. Our SLO team will be around the stadium before and during the game, look out for them or our 'Here To Help' team - they will all be clearly identified. We have a matchday familiarisation opportunity for any supporters who are new to the stadium - this is free and there is no need to sign up, simply head to the ticket office for 1.15pm. The below video will help you plan your journey to the game - click here to view our full guide for first-time fans. This content is from an external website which may store  cookies you have not consented to. Supporters wanting to access the tunnel area pre-match can collect wristbands from the club shop on a first come, first served basis. The Imps provide a free audio descriptive commentary service for fans with visual impairments. Headsets and receivers can be collected from the ticket office before the game (from the SLO point 12noon-1.30pm, then from the ticket office desks). Fans are encouraged to bring their own headphones where possible to minimise the amount of equipment needed to be shared - the receivers have a standard aux output. Anyone with questions about the service are asked to contact disability liaison officer Heidi Langham on dlo@theredimps.com. Official teamsheets are available from the Red Imps Community Trust pod in the Fan Village or from the Club Shop around 2.15pm. These cost 50p. Tickets cost just £1 and give three chances of winning, with our seven tickets for £5 offer in place for the best value chance to win. Would you like to win a cash prize or take home a unique piece of Imps memorabilia? Look out for the Fun Farm Imps Superdraw sellers around the ProAmpac Stadium. Please note that payment is only accepted via card or other contactless options. Parking on the South Common car park is available to supporters - click HERE to purchase. Fewer than 150 tickets were remaining for Saturday's fixture as of Friday lunchtime. Don't miss out - click HERE to purchase. Please note that screenshots of digital tickets are not permitted - entrance will only be permitted with tickets in the Ticketmaster all or phone ticket app such as Apple Wallet or Google Wallet. We offer an anonymous online form for supporters to report any concerns around safety or inappropriate behaviour and chanting in or around the stadium. Use the QR code which is situated around the stadium or click here. Our unisex accessible toilets can be found in each corner of the ProAmpac Stadium, as well as each bar and hospitality suite. Supporters can find them on the stadium map and signposted with toilet icons in and around the ProAmpac Stadium. These toilets also include baby changing facilities. We would like to make supporters aware of new legislation which requires the football club to separate waste. In order to apply, clearly designated bins will be located throughout the stadium. Please help us keep the ProAmpac Stadium clean and tidy by putting your rubbish in the correct bin. Like every business throughout the country, the Imps are now required by law to comply with new waste regulations, failure to do so will result in the club receiving a fine. Thank you to all supporters in advance for their understanding and cooperation with this matter. Every fan should feel safe and enjoy an inclusive experience when they attend matches at the ProAmpac Stadium and dangerous or anti-social behaviour have no place in our game - with significant consequences possible for fans who commit pitch incursions. City joined other EFL clubs in the Love Football, Protect the Game campaign to educate supporters on the impact of anti-social behaviour and pitch incursions which can result in banning orders for the individuals concerned and significant fines being imposed on the club by the football authorities. Regulation changes and tough new measures have been introduced which will see people who are found to have committed offences face stadium bans and potential criminal prosecution. The game will also continue its efforts to combat dangerous, illegal and unwelcome behaviour off the pitch, be it in the stands or online. Last season a host of new measures were introduced by authorities which saw enhanced sanctions applied for people identified entering the pitch, using pyros, taking drugs to games, throwing objects or for discriminatory abuse. Supporters are reminded that the ProAmpac Stadium is cashless across all hospitality and concession areas. Last season, 91% of transactions across the stadium were made by card or contactless, with just 9% made in cash. The significant majority of cash transactions were made in the club shop, often for larger ticketing or retail purchases. Following a full review of payment methods across the stadium, and with the aim of providing a quicker and more efficient service for supporters during busy periods before kick-off and at half-time, all hospitality and concession units will move to card and contactless payments only. The club shop and ticket office will continue to have a cash till for supporters who wish to make retail or ticket purchases in cash. Supporters can pay with all major debit and credit cards, as well as Apple Pay and Google Pay.

title: Is el clásico still the world’s biggest match? Three questions before Barcelona v Real Madrid - The Guardian
content: The fixture’s relevance waned as the Messi-Ronaldo rivalry faded. Can Lamine Yamal and Mbappé lift it into a new era? For the best part of a decade, el clásico was more than just soccer’s biggest fixture. It was the defining narrative. At the peak of the Lionel Messi v Cristiano Ronaldo era, there were clásicos everywhere. Yes, when the two historic rivals clashed on the pitch, but also in the voting for the Ballon d’Or every year and in so much of the discourse around the sport. As the Messi-Ronaldo rivalry faded, though, so too did the clásico’s relevance. This isn’t to say matches between Barcelona and Real Madrid no longer matter. They always have and always will. In 2026, however, it’s difficult to measure a clásico’s standing. Is it still the sport’s biggest fixture? Sunday’s match at Camp Nou will be watched by hundreds of millions of viewers all over the world. A clásico always carries significance, but this weekend’s edition will be especially significant. A Barça win would move them nine points clear of their rivals at the top of La Liga. A Real Madrid victory could be a catalyst for the rest of their season. Lamine Yamal may be the best player in the world right now, and he could have the Ballon d’Or trophy to prove it by Monday. Kylian Mbappé is up there too. The Clásico doesn’t lack for star power, but the framing of the fixture has changed in recent times. Not so long ago, the world stopped to watch it. Now, the world doesn’t seem so bothered. Unless Manchester City’s financial rule-breaking has a tangible effect on the Premier League’s reputation, the English top flight remains soccer’s dominant league. The league with more fans around the world than any other. A behemoth so omnipresent that even the uninterested are at least aware. April’s title clash between Manchester City and Arsenal set a new record as the most-watched Premier League match in US TV history, nearly doubling the mark for the most-watched clásico in US TV history set in October 2025. Audience trends point towards the Premier League being European soccer’s most compelling product. The packaging of the division is possibly part of this. While La Liga has bounced between different broadcasters, the Premier League made a long-term commitment to Sky Sports in the UK and NBC in the USA to properly broadcast and promote matches. Premier League matches are filmed with more cameras. They look better. More vibrant. It also helps that fans know where to consistently find games in their TV guide. La Liga has tried to broaden its global appeal, setting up an office in New York and even floating the idea of playing a competitive match in Miami. Past clásico encounters have been scheduled for a primetime audience in Asia. The Premier League, however, has the advantage of being an English language-first league which appears to be an advantage in the modern media market. At the peak of the clásico’s relevance, there was an unavoidable sense that the fixture was a showcase for the very best that the sport had to offer. That, however, is no longer the case. Barcelona are Europe’s most exhilarating team to watch, but the inherent chaos of their playing style under Hansi Flick comes with problems (primarily their high defensive line) that have prevented them from truly challenging for the Champions League. It’s been a full decade since Barça last won the Champions League. While Real Madrid have enjoyed continental glory more recently, winning a 14th European Cup in 2024, they are a long way from being the team who dominated Europe under Carlo Ancelotti and Zinedine Zidane. Real Madrid find themselves behind the curve of the modern game and the appointment of José Mourinho in the summer didn’t change that. If anything, the Special One’s not-so-special return to the Santiago Bernabéu has highlighted the club’s stagnancy. Xabi Alonso dared to introduce new ideas and was hounded out for it. Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Instead, Paris Saint-Germain are setting the standard at the top of the game – and doing so with a former Barcelona player and manager at the helm. And with a former Barcelona forward performing a false-nine role pioneered by Messi. Lamine Yamal has 20 goal contributions in just 12 games for Barcelona this season. Mbappé has 15 in the same number of games for Real Madrid. Both players represent a new direction for their respective teams and could dominate the clásico as individuals for years in the way Messi and Ronaldo did. Perhaps Sunday’s encounter will be the first truly memorable clash between the two. Vinícius Júnior is suspended while Raphinha is only just returning to fitness after a minor muscle injury, meaning there will be even more focus on Mbappé and Lamine Yamal. Messi scored 26 clásico goals, the most of any player in the fixture’s history. Ronaldo had the second most (18), tied with Alfredo Di Stéfano. Mbappé and Lamine Yamal have a long way to go to reach such heights as the two new faces of Spain’s Big Two, but with every meeting their personal rivalry will grow. The narrative will build. Meaning comes out of history. Shared experience. A consensus that something matters can take time to be reached and while the consensus is that Mbappé and Lamine Yamal are two of the best players in the world, their careers have yet to be intertwined as two rivals whose story can only be told as one. When that happens, the clásico may reclaim its status as soccer’s most meaningful game.

title: The 1980 Triumph TR8 Was a $13,000 V-8 Sports Car That Proved Shockingly Good - MotorTrend
content: A 20,000-mile durability run to find out whether a British V-8 sports car really is competition for the sophisticated products from the Germans and the Japanese. [This story originally appeared in the February 1981 issue of Motor Trend with the headline "Triumph TR8," and comes from a time when we had a space in our name.] That a strange turn of events. With the introduction of one new model—based on a car that’s been around for five years—the British are back in the sports car business. Not that they've actually been out of it, just away from it by trying to maintain their "classic" posture while German and Japanese competition has been dishing out overhead cam and independent suspension technology to a public that has had its performance rug jerked from under it. But in one well-executed move, Triumph is back on top, providing a true Performance Sports Car at a Right Price, and for that Triumph deserves our thanks. Its ace in the hole is a basic hot-rodding staple—the old stuff-in-an-American-V-8-engine trick, done about as well as anyone has done it. The engine is the 215-cubic-inch aluminum V-8 that General Motors tried to sell us in Buick Skylarks and Oldsmobile F-85s in the early '60s. But we Americans didn't need economy in those cheap-gas days, nor were we attracted to a V-8 that was smaller in displacement than most of our 6-cylinder engines. So the engine design and production tooling were eventually sold to British Leyland, who used the little V-8 in Rover models, adding it to the Triumph line this year. And judging by the results, the TR8 is the car this engine has been waiting for. In the TR8, Triumph has produced a sports car like no other available today for anywhere near its price, a car with handling, power, style, and fun, fun, fun. It's one of those automotive rarities that makes driving so enjoyable that you think of places to go just for the pleasure of being in the car. Like most cars, it has its odd characteristics and even a few faults, but they're so outweighed by good qualities they become minor. In more than 21,000 miles, our TR8 had only one recurring problem: an overenthusiastic alternator/regulator that overcharged the battery to the point of boiling away the battery's electrolyte, requiring regular and very frequent addition of water to the battery cells. None of the Triumph dealers who worked on the car was able to overcome the difficulty. The alternator would be tested, found to be producing the factory-specified 14.2 volts, and declared to be in sound working order. No test was available for the alternator's built-in regulator, so that the 14.2 volts were being delivered almost constantly to the battery through the faulty regulator, rather than being shunted off to ground when the battery reached its full storage capacity. The situation had a definite Catch-22 quality—there was apparently no factory-authorized test for this type of regulator problem, and no parts could be replaced on warranty without the problem being identified by a test. One Triumph service representative’s suggestion: drive with the headlights on to consume some of the excess current to slow down the overcharging Not exactly the cure you'd hope for with a new $13,000 car, but it did help. That is, until the regulator changed its tack one day and decided not to charge at all, allowing the battery to go completely dead in the mountains of western Canada. After a battery charge, the alternator was back to its old trick of steadily overcharging. Even dismantling the alternator for inspection and testing by a Lucas repair shop didn't isolate the cause, so the rot-ten-eggs odor of the sulfur fumes from the trunk-mounted battery became a part of our Triumph's personality. The battery's ventilation system was unable to handle the vapors that filled the trunk and occasionally leaked into the passenger compartment of the car. Something of a hassle? Yes. But the rest of the car made it all worthwhile. The fun was in the engine, its performance, and the car's handling. It's been a long time since there was an affordable sports car with the power to really accelerate out of a turn, and the TR8 does that as a way of life. The 148 horsepower from the fuel-injected engine (California version) and the car's weight of just over 2600 pounds is a combination you can't soon forget and just one of the ways the TR8 has been developed into an extremely well-balanced package. The power is delivered over a broad rpm range; the car takes off almost as nimbly in 2nd gear as in 1st and will drive away in 5th gear from less than 1000 rpm (about 20 mph) with never a hesitation or any sign of pre-ignition. Acceleration is spirited in every gear; the TR8 won't blow the doors off a 427 Camaro; but the way the car feels, you wouldn't know that until you've tried. The power is delivered with electric motor quiet and smoothness, a quality that adds to the car's feeling of performance. At highway speeds, the quiet is deceiving. It's hard to believe the speedometer—70 feels like 55, 55 like 35. Considering the performance the engine gives, it asks very little. At highway speeds, it easily delivers 25-26 mpg and is capable of 30 mpg on flat terrain. Even during periods of extended high-rpm, full-throttle driving, the mileage never dropped below 19 mpg, through 21,000 miles. Around town, the injected TR8 engine will deliver 21-22 mpg, well above its EPA figure of 16 mpg. Oil consumption was consistently one quart per 3,000 miles of driving. The engine in our test car was the California version which features Bosch-Lucas electronic fuel injection, very similar in design to that used by Porsche. Only the California cars were fuel injected for 1980 as a means to meet the state's more stringent emissions requirements. All other TR8s are fitted with dual Zenith sidedraft carbs that give the engine a more typically British look and offer only 133 horsepower, marking this as one of the few times in recent years that the California cars haven't suffered because of the state's more restrictive emissions laws. For 1981 all TR8s will be injected. In actual driving feel, one would be hard pressed to tell an injected TR8 from a carbureted one. Both are smooth and powerful, and both exhibit the same broad torque range. The biggest difference is the wonderful whistle that comes from the fuel injection's air intake, a sound that rises and falls with the engine rpm, adding not a grain of real performance but serving as a constant reminder that this is no ordinary sports car. Handling is the other area where the TR8 shines. It corners like a go-kart and has an almost computer-like straight tracking ability. The car has the power to take you into a corner thinking you may be going just a little too fast, yet it has the handling to bring you out of the corner thinking you could have done it at twice the speed. Initially, the rack-and-pinion power steering seems almost too quick, only takes a few corners to convince you that it's just right. It has no obvious pow-er-assisted feeling, giving the impression of manual steering the way you always dreamed it could be-just the right amount of steering wheel resistance to let you know exactly what the front wheels are doing. It's an easy car to drive at almost any speed. After a week in the car, one of the staffers rightly called it a perfect American sports car. Underneath the sheet metal is a chassis that is as American as base-ball, apple pie, and all that other stuff. It's a front-engine rear-wheel-drive car with independent front suspension and a coil-sprung, non-independent rear end And it drives like you would expect an American car to drive, only better. It's one of those cars that makes you wonder why other cars aren't just like it. Anyone raised on conventional rear-wheel-drive American cars will feel right at home in the TR, and that's a big part of its immediate charm. It doesn't have any unusual quirks; it goes where you want it predictably and effortlessly. The TR8 maintained its on-a-rail handling characteristics for just over 17,000 miles, at which point the shock absorbers began to exhibit signs of rapid wear. After being able to drive the car fast through unfamiliar corners with a high degree of confidence and almost effortless control, the car began to lean in hard turns and we had a difficult time keeping the rear tires pressed against the pavement. By 20,000 miles, our control and confidence were gone to the extent that even familiar turns required an unusual amount of braking and produced a high level of anxiety. Where it had initially been difficult to break the rear end of the car loose in a turn by applying throttle, it became a problem keeping the rear end following the front end through a fast turn. And at higher speeds the car developed a telltale side-to-side wallow in contrast to its former rock-steady ride. The car finally felt like the 85-inch-wheelbase vehicle it is. This would be, in fact, the case with most cars; 20,000 miles is a fair amount to get from the original equipment shocks on nearly any car. It's just that the TR8 is a far better handling car than most, and when the shocks go, the change is far more dramatic. The car simply has more handling to lose than most cars. We replaced only the rear shocks with a fresh pair of original-equipment Triumph shocks at 20,000 miles, and the handling improved to about 65–70% of its original form. A very fair investment after 20,000 miles of driving fun; for about $100 worth of parts, the Fun To Drive flag flew again. And if you want to regain the rest of the handling, the front shocks are easy to find. Mechanically, the TR8s only shortcoming is its brakes. Though Triumph is quick to point out that the brakes have been upgraded from those on the 4-cylinder TR7, they still aren't enough for the performance of the TR8. They're not bad brakes, please understand; they're only good brakes, and the car needs more. They're not the type that make you think, "Wow, how did I ever stop that quickly?" Instead they leave you more with a thankful, "Whew, I made it," feeling. The car does stop very straight but with a lot of pedal pressure and occasional locking of the rear brakes. It's really the only point where the car's performance is unbalanced—there's a lot more engine than brakes. The TR8 is certainly a much faster car than the Volkswagen Vanagon or the Toyota Tercel, but it won't stop as quickly as either. It should be pointed out that when the shocks are in shape the car corners so well you find yourself using the brakes sparingly in all but the most aggressive driving situations. It's too bad there wasn't the budget for 4-wheel discs to make the TR8 the total performance car it so very nearly is. Which brings up the big question-how fast does it go? Gas station attendants and interested onlookers generally perceived the TR8 as a 140–160-mph vehicle, no doubt influenced by the intimidating array of tubing adorning the top of the engine. No matter to them that it's only a 215-cubic-inch engine. The engine redlines at 5,500 rpm with peak horsepower (148) reached at 5,100. In the first three gears, the engine will blaze past 5,500, losing horsepower but still winding like it has somewhere important to go. The federally mandated 85-mph speedometer pegs just before the 5,500 redline in 3rd gear. The car accelerates hard again in 4th gear to just over 100 before wind resistance and the small displacement begin to slow the rate of acceleration. In top-speed runs with about 6000 miles and again with about 13,000 miles on the car, both at road elevations of around 4,000 feet, the engine would not pull redline in 4th gear, flattening out at 5,200 rpm. In 5th, wind resistance ended things once at 112, then again at 117 mph. Later, with more than 21,000 miles on the odometer and on a road near sea level, the engine pulled its 5,500 redline in 4th and powered to 5,000 rpm in 5th gear, a speed of over 123 mph. And it's a nice ride, stable and quiet, though the speed builds slowly above 110. But it's that charge to 100 that hasn't been felt from many cars in a long while! Throughout our test, the TR8’s interior remained one of the most comfortable in smallcardom. The seats offer a wide range of adjustment, fore and aft and seat back angle, and a good amount of leg room. Our test car was air conditioned, a feature many people found humorous for a convertible, but a necessary one in all but the coldest climates if only to overcome the deficiencies of the Triumph's ventilation system. In the short amount of time it takes for air to move from the intake vents at the rear of the hood to the car's interior, the air is exposed to enough engine heat to raise the air temperature past the point of being refreshing. Even if the outside air is crisp and cool, the air being blown through the dash vents will be decidedly warm. And if the outside air slightly warm, you'll think the heater is on. Roll down the window, you say? Not quite that easy. The slippery shape of the front end directs the air around the sides so effectively that barely a whisper of breeze will enter through the side windows. That's part of the reason the Triumph interior is so free of wind noise-this Triumph convertible is actually quieter insıde than many sedans, thanks to the car's aerodynamics and to the well-fitting top. You can stick your hand a half-inch outside the window line and feel the cool air you're praying for, but it's near impossible to get it into the car. It's mainly a problem down in the footwells where there is very little circulation and the last thing you need is warm air. The small windwing-style pieces of glass in the doors unfortunately are fixed in place. If they swiveled open as they did in older cars, you would be able to get some outside air to the interior. But this is a convertible after all, and real ventilation is only moments away. The top works quickly and easily (manually, not electrically), and the whole process, including installing or removing the boot, can be done in three minutes. This gives you maximum Wind In The Hair and great visibility (to see or be seen as needed). A middle-of-the-road option that is a wonderful compromise is running with the top up and the rear window zipped open. The air curls over the roof and into the open rear window, providing good circulation with little direct wind. The air conditioning itself is an effective unit, a Delco (American) compressor that can normally cool the interior almost instantly. The only time the air conditioning met its match was in the 110-degree heat of a Central California summer, when it was able to keep the interior bearable but never actually cool. Most of the time, it was as good as you'd want; the humid 95-degree Midwest was a piece of cake for the system. Its only curious feature was the control that regulated the amount of cold air the system produced. Since the single lever controlled both the heater temperature and the cycling of the air conditioning compressor, it was possible to turn on both the heater and the A/C at the same time. The A/C compressor would be cycling on and off, as it should, to give the desired amount of cool air from the dash vents, but the heater would also go on, steadily blowing warm air into the footwells. And it's tough to feel cool when your feet are hot. The only answer was to leave the temperature control in the cold position and let the air conditioning compressor run constantly. This eliminates the heater from the A/C system but also eliminates the possibility of any fine adjusting of the interior temperature by cycling the A/C compressor on and off. It's a basic design flaw and could be easily corrected, but isn't this a part of what people love about British cars? Though we were able to put 1–1½ years of mileage on a car in a matter of a few months, there is no way to reproduce the effects time will have on components such as the interior, paint, and convertible top. In our months in the TR8, the interior proved extremely comfortable and as durable as one has a right to expect. The only problem with the upholstery in our car was a strip of fabric that loosened from the metal frame above the windshield, a simple gluing job requiring only minutes to repair. The narrow but very comfortable bucket seats were upholstered in a cloth/vinyl combination, the cloth being the plaid fabric that is part of the traditional British Sports Car pose. While most people found the plaid pattern rather distracting, the cooler fabric inserts were certainly preferable to vinyl for seats exposed to direct sunlight when the convertible top is down. The top itself fit extremely well, yet not so tight that putting the top up became a wrestling match. Two of the convertible top's eight snap fasteners were damaged early in the car's stay with us. One snap, of a plastic/metal construction, broke away a section of its plastic; another ripped or was ripped loose from the top fabric, perhaps by someone in too much of a hurry to enjoy the wind in the hair. Neither mishap impaired the top's ability to function or caused leakage or wind noise problems. The only water leaks were at two points where the front corners of the top met the doors and windshield frame, and where gaps large enough to easily slip a pencil through would let a small amount of water drip onto the front of each seat during car washes. The amount of water let in was minimal, however, and the gaps let no water through during even very heavy rains. The overall fit of the top was such that most people who rode in the car commented on the quiet. Even at the end of our test, though the fabric top had stretched and softened slightly, the car remained free of wind noise. One surprising part of the interior was the dashboard. It was, as in most new cars, a study in 1,001 Things to Do With Plastic, but it remained rattle- and squeak-free throughout our test, even though the car was driven on some roads that would shake the tracks off a tank. One of the instrument cluster's Too Many idiot lights, this one scheduled to come on at about 22,000 miles to remind us to have the catalytic converter serviced, lit up at about 4,500 miles. Triumph advised us to disconnect the wire from the light, but since it was well enough blocked from view by the thick rim of the steering wheel, we let it go. At about 18,600 miles, the light, went off as mysteriously as it had come on. The instruments are well placed and easy to read, but since the TR8 is unavoidably destined to have a performance image. either the clock or the voltmeter should be replaced by an oil pressure gauge. Part of the car's standard equipment package is an AM/FM stereo radio. Our car's radio included the optional tape player, which we don't recommend—put your money into something you can use, like the. Brooklyn Bridge. By 15,000 miles, we were on our third radio/tape unit, each having failed for a different reason. When the third one quit, we quit caring. You can get a far better piece of audio equipment for your money in the aftermarket than is provided as original equipment by the car maker. The tires on our test car, Michelin 185/13 radials on cast alloy wheels, gripped the road very well on both wet and dry surfaces. At about 9,700 miles, the normally steady steering wheel developed a slight shake at 50-55 mph. The shake increased as the mileage increased, but was only noticeable in that same 5-mph increment. Spin-balancing the front wheels completely eliminated the shake, but one of the front tires required two ounces of balancing weight, a rather large amount for such a small tire. The only time the wheel/tire combination was a negative factor in the car's performance was on stretches of particularly rough road where the small-diameter tires (23 inches) tended to fall into holes and depressions in the road that a larger-diameter tire would have rolled over. During the 21,000 miles of testing, the tires did not lose a single pound of air. Our TR8 test car with its optional air conditioning had a list price of just over $13,000. If you choke at that, chances are you're simply out of touch with the reality of what cars cost today. A similarly equipped Corvette costs $15,000, doesn't go as fast as the Triumph or get as good gas mileage, and isn't available as a convertible. A vastly slower VW Rabbit convertible with the same equipment $10,000. The only other V-8 sports car, short of the ’Vette, is the Porsche 928, a wonderful automobile, far more sophisticated than the TR8, but at $38,000 it's not three times better. As for convertibles, there aren't any others that are affordable. Don’t just think of the TR8 as a $13,000 Triumph; think of it as an aluminum-engined, fuel-injected, V-8-powered convertible sports car that does just about everything right. If you buy any sports car in the $9,000–17,000 price range without taking a test drive in a TR8, you'll have done yourself a real disservice. It certainly supplies more than $13,000 worth of fun. The only maintenance the car ever wanted, needed or got was regular lubrication and oil/filter changes. From sea level to over 9,000-feet elevation, the engine never missed, pinged or complained It was never tuned during its stay with us and made its 123-mph run on spark plugs that had been in the engine for more than 21,000 miles, having been regapped only once at 17,000 miles. The engine felt like it wanted to go 40,000 miles on the original plugs. Through its 21,000 miles. the TR8 powerplant would have to be considered a marvel of low maintenance. As common as Triumphs are in most urban areas, it's a whole new story once you're into rural America. A great many people reacted to the TR8 as if it were a Ferrari or something much more exotic than it is. People would turn and watch as it passed them on the street, often not moving until the car was out of sight. Many seemed to have no idea what kind of car it was. Even after they read the 4-inch-high letters on the back spelling TRIUMPH, they would ask, "Hey buddy, what kinda car ya drivin' here? Wherezit made?" If they ventured a guess, the first would always be that the car was German. And many people were sure they'd never seen one of the five-year-old cars before. Perhaps it was the convertible version that made it seem so totally new. One person slightly familiar with the cars observed that they looked so right as convertibles that they must have been originally designed that way, then changed to hardtops at the last minute, when in actuality, it happened just the other way around. But he was right. The car is more visually comfortable as a convertible. All in all, Triumph's TR8 is a very nice car. One driver who put many miles on our test vehicle said that if he had been in the market for a sports car before his TR8 experience, he probably wouldn't have even considered a Triumph. But after driving the TR8, his former first choice became a very distant second. The TR-8 is a major step forward for Triumph and is a car unique to its price class. title: Alexander Isak interview: Goals, fitness and previewing Liverpool v Brighton - Liverpool FC
content:
Alexander Isak is relishing the challenge Liverpool will face when Brighton & Hove Albion visit Anfield. Two in-form teams clash on Sunday afternoon as the Reds, having won three consecutive games across all competitions, host the Seagulls, who have reeled off four Premier League victories in a row while scoring 15 goals and conceding zero. The game has all the hallmarks of a potential thriller, then, and Isak told Liverpoolfc.com: “It’s definitely one of the tougher opponents that you have in the league but I think in the Premier League in today’s football, there are no easy games. “So, I don’t think you need any motivation to do that, I think it’s already there. We know it’s going to be tough, but we play at home and we have to go to win.” After missing two games due to injury, Isak returned to Liverpool’s starting XI for last weekend’s trip to Brentford and duly scored the winner to earn a hard-fought 2-1 victory. The No.9 then came off the bench during Tuesday’s Champions League defeat of Villarreal and said he ‘feels good’. Isak added: “It was a short time I was out so I don’t feel like I’ve missed too much, so I feel good. It feels like the team is in a good place so yeah, excited.” The Sweden striker has scored five goals in six Premier League appearances so far this season, with four of those directly responsible for securing wins away to Ipswich Town, AFC Bournemouth and Brentford. When asked if he has specific goal targets in mind, he replied: “No, not really. Just try to be on the scoresheet for every game and try to make them count as important ones as well.” The Reds have scored 12 times in their last three outings and Isak believes there is even more to come from the attacking unit. “I think the potential is super-high, which is good because I think we can do much better as well so the ceiling is definitely high,” he said. All three have the ability to hit the ball beautifully, but are there stats to confirm which of these greats hits the ball best? When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works. When it comes to considering results in the men’s professional game, Tiger Woods is clearly ahead of both Rory McIlroy and Scottie Scheffler. He has 82 PGA Tour titles to his name, including 15 Majors. He’s won a total of 110 professional tournaments. McIlroy has claimed 30 PGA Tour titles, six Majors and a total of 45 wins as a pro. Scheffler has 22 PGA Tour wins, four Majors and 27 pro wins in total. Okay, Jack has more Majors, but, for me, Woods is the greatest winner in the history of the men’s game. He was quite simply a machine in his prime. But has he been the best ball-striker? Others would certainly have a claim to that title. I once watched Sandy Lyle hit 25 3-woods on the driving range at Carnoustie. I’ve never seen better ball-striking than that. Hogan, Nelson, Nicklaus, Snead – all were famous as amazing strikers of the golf ball. What about Moe Norman, the Canadian with the unusual action who hit every ball arrow straight and only went out of bounds once in his career? So, Woods has stiff competition. And what about the two best in the modern game, Scheffler and McIlroy – what do the statistics say about their ball striking in comparison to Tiger? Well, through the 2026 season, Scottie Scheffler has led the ball striking statistics category on the PGA Tour. That category adds a player’s ranking in the total driving category (that’s distance combined with accuracy) to their ranking in the greens in regulation (GIR) category to give a total, ball striking value. In 2026, Scottie’s value is 9 – seventh in driving, second in GIR. Rory McIlroy is way down in 56th on the ranking with a value of 117 – 62nd in total driving and 55th in GIR. Rory hits it miles off the tee, but he doesn’t hit it very straight. Over the last five seasons, McIlroy has ranked 9th, 59th, 62nd, 78th then 56th in the ball- striking category. Scheffler has been 4th, 3rd, 1st, 6th and 1st. Using the criteria the PGA Tour use to define ball-striking, Scheffler blows Rory out of the water. And Tiger? Well, let’s consider him at his best, say the five years from 2000-2004. During that period, Woods ranked 1st, 12th, 2nd and 27th, 61st. In fact, if you look back through the years, Woods has only once led the ball-striking stat – his amazing 2000 season. But is that the right way to define ball striking? Simply by the results? Surely the purity of the strike, the quality of and control over the ball flight and the sound at impact must be taken into account? That’s a little more difficult to quantify. Smash factor gives a good indication – a measure of how efficient you are at transferring energy from the clubhead into the ball. It is calculated by dividing the ball speed by the clubhead speed. Rory has a smash factor of 1.508 with a driver and keeps it at up to 1.5 with his longer irons – he has had shots measured with a 7-iron where he recorded 1.50. Scheffler is well down on smash factor – he has an average with the driver of 1.4878. With a 7-iron, he’s been measured at 1.43. Tiger was using different equipment in his prime and launch data didn’t exist at the time of his legendary 2000 season. There are records, though, of him testing at the Nike facility where he was recorded as hitting an iron with a smash factor of 1.50. When it comes to smash factor, it would go to either Rory or Tiger. When one considers pure control of the golf ball, I think Tiger has to win. In terms of his ability to shape the ball, control the flight and move it both ways, not many in the history of the game could match Tiger. In my opinion, Tiger is the best ball-striker of the three. I once saw him hit a stinger 2-iron, again at Carnoustie, that was the most purely struck golf shot I have ever witnessed. The stats on ball-striking and smash factor may favour Scheffler and McIlroy, but for me, in terms of the sound, quality of impact and control of ball flight, Tiger Woods was in a league of his own.
